'''Naomi Livesay''' (1916{{snd}}2001) was an American mathematician who contributed to the [[Manhattan Project]]. She received her bachelor's degree in mathematics from [[Cornell College]] in Iowa and went on to receive a Ph.M. in mathematics from the [[University of Wisconsin]] in 1939. Livesay worked on the Manhattan Project at Los Alamos from 1944-1946 where she was assigned to calculate the predicted shockwave propulsion from an implosion type bomb.

== Early life and education ==
Naomi Mary Livesay was born in northern [[Montana]] in 1916.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Hafner |first1=Katie |title=Meet the Woman Who Supervised the Computations That Proved an Atomic Bomb Would Work |url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/meet-the-woman-who-supervised-the-computations-that-proved-an-atomic-bomb-would-work/ |work=Scientific American |date=August 3, 2023 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |title=Directory of Fellowship Awards for the Years 1922-1950 |date=1952 |publisher=General Education Board |page=69 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=V2pqAAAAMAAJ&q=%22naomi%20livesay%22 |language=en}}</ref> She earned her B.A. in mathematics from [[Cornell College]] in Iowa and was elected to [[Phi Beta Kappa]].<ref>{{cite news |title=Phi Beta Kappa Spring Election Honors 6 Seniors |work=The Cornellian |date=April 13, 1937 |page=1}}</ref> Afterwards, she went on to the [[University of Wisconsin]] where she was a research assistant in the education department. Due to discrimination against women at the school, she was prevented from pursuing her Ph.D. Instead she earned her Ph.M. in mathematics in 1939.<ref name="Howes2003">{{cite book |last1=Howes |first1=Ruth H. |last2=Herzenberg |first2=Caroline L. |title=Their Day in the Sun: Women of the Manhattan Project |date=2003 |publisher=Temple University Press |isbn=978-1-59213-192-1 |pages=104–109 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Ys0N4rFgt6UC&dq=%22naomi%20livesay%22&pg=PA104 |language=en}}</ref>

==Career==
Upon receiving her Ph.M. in mathematics, Livesay worked at [[Princeton University]]'s [[Princeton School of Public and International Affairs|School of Public and International Affairs]] where she worked for Princeton Surveys, calculating statistics regarding the costs of state and local governments.<ref name="Howes2003"/> She went to Philadelphia where she was trained in the operation and programming of IBM Punch-Card Accounting Machines (PCAMs).<ref name="Archer2021">{{cite journal |last1=Archer |first1=B. J. |title=The Los Alamos Computing Facility During the Manhattan Project |journal=Nuclear Technology |date=3 December 2021 |volume=207 |issue=sup1 |pages=S197–S199 |doi=10.1080/00295450.2021.1940060 |arxiv=2103.05705 |bibcode=2021NucTe.207S.190A |url=https://www.osti.gov/servlets/purl/1837001v}}</ref> She had an assistant and designed plug-board programs for the device for six months. Livesay then received a [[Rockefeller Foundation]] fellowship to study education at the [[University of Chicago]]. She worked with [[Bruno Bettelheim]] and George Sheviakov on a psychology project.<ref name="Howes2003"/>

Shortly after, in fall 1940, she began assistant teaching at the [[University of Illinois]], where she was promoted to a full-time instructor the following academic year.<ref name="AHF" />

===Manhattan Project===
[[File:IBM 601 - MfK Bern.jpg|thumb|Livesay programmed [[IBM 601]]s and other PCAMs for the Manhattan Project.]]
Livesay was brought onto the [[Manhattan Project]] by American physicist [[Joseph O. Hirschfelder|Joseph Hirschfelder]] where he initially reached out to her with the opportunity in the fall of 1943. She began work at Los Alamos in February 1944 after receiving her security clearance. Her advanced mathematics degree and training in programming IBM machines made her uniquely qualified. Upon her arrival, Livesay was asked to work for [[Richard Feynman]]'s theoretical group, working to determine the predicted shock wave that would result from an implosion type bomb.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=No Place for a Woman in Mathematics? The Woman Who Ended up Supervising The Computations that Proved an Atomic Bomb Would Work |url=https://www.lostwomenofscience.org/season-6-episodes/no-place-for-a-woman-in-mathematics-the-woman-who-ended-up-supervising-the-computations-that-proved-an-atomic-bomb-would-work |access-date=2024-04-16 |website=www.lostwomenofscience.org |language=en}}</ref> Livesay held a supervisor role on Feynman's team where she oversaw a crew that ran IBM machines 24 hours a day. She also performed hand calculations to check the work of the IBM machine.<ref name="AHF" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Lewis |first=N. |date=2021-12-03 |title=Trinity by the Numbers: The Computing Effort that Made Trinity Possible |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00295450.2021.1938487 |journal=Nuclear Technology |language=en |volume=207 |issue=sup1 |pages=S176–S189 |doi=10.1080/00295450.2021.1938487 |arxiv=2103.06211 |bibcode=2021NucTe.207S.176L |issn=0029-5450}}</ref>

Alongside [[Stan Frankel]] and Eldred Nelson, Livesay developed a program for the PCAMs to solve the set of hydrodynamic equations for implosions in February and March of 1944. She later served as supervisor of the PCAM operators.<ref name="Archer2021"/> Livesay recruited mathematician Eleanor Ewing to the project. While at Los Alamos, they both received mathematics lectures from [[John von Neumann]]. Livesay, in turn, instructed von Neumann in the use of the IBM machines, information that he later used in the design of [[ENIAC]].<ref name="Howes2003"/>

After the Manhattan Project, Livesay attempted to continue her career in England. She worked to establish a computer link between Harwell and Teddington. Her salary, 30 percent below that of her colleagues,<ref>{{cite book |last1=Hughes |first1=William |title=Annual Editions: Western Civilization |date=1995 |publisher=Dushkin Publishing Group |isbn=978-1-56134-375-1 |page=178 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=eNXOHzhfqKYC&q=%22naomi%20livesay%22 |language=en}}</ref> did not sufficiently offset expense of child care and she abandoned her mathematics career.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Jardins |first1=Julie Des |title=The Madame Curie Complex: The Hidden History of Women in Science |date=2010 |publisher=The Feminist Press at CUNY |isbn=978-1-55861-655-4 |pages=126 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=HULGDNDSenYC&dq=%22naomi%20livesay%22&pg=PA126 |language=en}}</ref> Beginning in 1956, she taught for a year as an assistant professor of science at [[Columbia College (South Carolina)|Columbia College]] in South Carolina.<ref>{{cite news |title=Science Teacher |work=The Index-Journal |date=September 20, 1956 |page=8}}</ref>

==Personal life==
While working at Los Alamos, Livesay met experimental nuclear physicist [[Anthony French]]. They married in October 1945 and had two children.<ref name="AHF" /> She died in [[Arlington, Massachusetts]], on March 6, 2001.<ref name="AHF">{{Cite web |title=Naomi Livesay - Nuclear Museum |url=https://ahf.nuclearmuseum.org/ahf/profile/naomi-livesay/ |access-date=2024-04-16 |publisher=Atomic Heritage Foundation |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Death notices: French |work=The Boston Globe |date=March 8, 2001 |page=B8}}</ref>
